claim: MicroRNA targets are often recognized through pairing between the miRNA seed region (nucleotides 2-7) and complementary sites within target mRNAs.
source: MicroRNA targets are often recognized through pairing between the miRNA seed region and complementary sites within target mRNAs
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Not all canonical miRNA binding sites are equally effective at mediating repression.
source: MicroRNA targets are often recognized through pairing between the miRNA seed region and complementary sites within target mRNAs, but not all of these canonical sites are equally effective
evidence: This claim is supported by the development of a model with 14 features to predict effectiveness, implying variation in site efficacy.

claim: Recently reported non-canonical miRNA binding sites do not mediate repression despite binding the miRNA.
source: Here, we show that recently reported non-canonical sites do not mediate repression despite binding the miRNA
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental datasets analyzed in Figure 1 and related figures.

claim: The vast majority of functional miRNA target sites are canonical.
source: which indicates that the vast majority of functional sites are canonical
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the finding that non-canonical sites do not mediate repression.

claim: The context++ model considers site type and 14 additional features to predict effectively targeted mRNAs.
source: This model, which considers site type and another 14 features to predict the most effectively targeted mRNAs
evidence: The model development is described in the Results section with specific features listed in Table 1.

claim: The context++ model performed significantly better than existing models.
source: This model, which considers site type and another 14 features to predict the most effectively targeted mRNAs, performed significantly better than existing models
evidence: Performance comparisons are shown in Figures 4 and 5 with statistical significance testing.

claim: The context++ model was as informative as the best high-throughput in vivo crosslinking approaches.
source: performed significantly better than existing models and was as informative as the best high-throughput in vivo crosslinking approaches
evidence: Comparisons with CLIP approaches are shown in Figure 6.

claim: The context++ model drives TargetScan version 7.0.
source: It drives the latest version of TargetScan (v7.0; targetscan.org)
evidence: The implementation is described in the Results section on TargetScan database.

claim: MicroRNAs are approximately 22-nucleotide RNAs that mediate post-transcriptional gene repression.
source: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are ∼22-nt RNAs that mediate post-transcriptional gene repression (Bartel, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous work.

claim: MicroRNAs function by pairing primarily with 3′ UTRs of target RNAs through Watson-Crick pairing between the miRNA seed (nucleotides 2-7) and complementary sites.
source: miRNAs function as sequence-specific guides, directing the silencing complex to transcripts, primarily through Watson–Crick pairing between the miRNA seed (miRNA nucleotides 2–7) and complementary sites within the 3′ untranslated regions (3′ UTRs) of target RNAs (Lewis et al., 2005; Bartel, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The miRNAs conserved to fish have been grouped into 87 families, each with a unique seed region.
source: The miRNAs conserved to fish have been grouped into 87 families, each with a unique seed region.
evidence: This is a factual statement about miRNA classification.

claim: Each conserved miRNA family has on average more than 400 conserved targeting interactions.
source: On average, each of these families has >400 conserved targeting interactions
evidence: This is cited from previous work (Friedman et al., 2009).

claim: Conserved miRNA targeting interactions involve most mammalian mRNAs.
source: together these interactions involve most mammalian mRNAs (Friedman et al., 2009)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Many nonconserved miRNA-mRNA interactions function to reduce mRNA levels and protein output.
source: In addition, many nonconserved interactions also function to reduce mRNA levels and protein output (Farh et al., 2005; Krutzfeldt et al., 2005; Lim et al., 2005; Baek et al., 2008; Selbach et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: MicroRNAs have been implicated in a wide range of biological processes in worms, flies, and mammals.
source: Accordingly, miRNAs have been implicated in a wide range of biological processes in worms, flies, and mammals (Kloosterman and Plasterk, 2006; Bushati and Cohen, 2007; Stefani and Slack, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The 8mer site is the most effective canonical site type, consisting of a Watson-Crick match to miRNA positions 2-8 with an A opposite position 1.
source: The most effective canonical site types, listed in order of decreasing preferential conservation and efficacy, are the 8mer site (Watson–Crick match to miRNA positions 2–8 with an A opposite position 1 [Lewis et al., 2005])
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous work.

claim: The 7mer-m8 site consists of a position 2-8 match to the miRNA.
source: 7mer-m8 site (position 2–8 match [Brennecke et al., 2005; Krek et al., 2005; Lewis et al., 2005])
evidence: This is a definition cited from previous work.

claim: The 7mer-A1 site consists of a position 2-7 match with an A opposite position 1.
source: 7mer-A1 site (position 2–7 match with an A opposite position 1 [Lewis et al., 2005])
evidence: This is a definition cited from previous work.

claim: The preference for an adenosine opposite miRNA position 1 is independent of the miRNA nucleotide identity.
source: Experiments have confirmed that the preference for an adenosine opposite position 1 is independent of the miRNA nucleotide identity (Grimson et al., 2007; Nielsen et al., 2007; Baek et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The preference for an adenosine opposite miRNA position 1 is due to specific recognition of the target adenosine within a binding pocket of Argonaute.
source: due to the specific recognition of the target adenosine within a binding pocket of Argonaute (Schirle et al., 2014)
evidence: This mechanistic explanation is cited from structural work.

claim: The 6mer site consists of a position 2-7 match to the miRNA and is associated with much lower efficacy than 7-8mer sites.
source: Two other canonical site types, each associated with weaker preferential conservation and much lower efficacy (Friedman et al., 2009), are the 6mer (position 2–7 match [Lewis et al., 2005])
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The offset-6mer site consists of a position 3-8 match to the miRNA and is associated with much lower efficacy than 7-8mer sites.
source: offset-6mer (position 3–8 match [Friedman et al., 2009])
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Pairing to the 3′ end of the miRNA can supplement canonical sites, but evidence for this is observed for no more than 5% of seed-matched sites.
source: Pairing to the 3′ end of the miRNA can supplement canonical sites, although evidence for the use of this 3′-supplementary pairing is observed for no more than 5% of the seed-matched sites (Brennecke et al., 2005; Lewis et al., 2005; Grimson et al., 2007; Friedman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from multiple previous studies.

claim: Very extensive pairing to the 3′ region of the miRNA can compensate for a wobble or mismatch to one of the seed positions.
source: For example, very extensive pairing to the 3′ region of the miRNA can compensate for a wobble or mismatch to one of the seed positions (Doench and Sharp, 2004; Brennecke et al., 2005; Bartel, 2009)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The two let-7 sites within the 3′ UTR of C. elegans lin-41 exemplify 3′-supplementary sites.
source: as exemplified by the two let-7 sites within the 3′ UTR of Caenorhabditis elegans lin-41 (Reinhart et al., 2000)
evidence: This is cited as a specific example from previous work.

claim: 3′-supplementary sites are exceedingly rare, with conserved miRNA families averaging less than 1 preferentially conserved 3′-supplementary site.
source: Although these 3′-supplementary sites can be detected above background when searching for preferentially conserved pairing configurations, they are exceedingly rare, with conserved miRNA families in mammals and nematodes each averaging <1 preferentially conserved 3′-supplementary site (Friedman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Centered sites have 11-12 contiguous Watson-Crick pairs to the center of the miRNA.
source: Other relatively rare, yet effective sites include centered sites, which have 11–12 contiguous Watson–Crick pairs to the center of the miRNA (Shin et al., 2010)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Cleavage sites have very extensive pairing required for Argonaute-catalyzed slicing of the mRNA.
source: cleavage sites, which have the very extensive pairing required for Argonaute-catalyzed slicing of the mRNA (Yekta et al., 2004; Davis et al., 2005; Karginov et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2010)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: A large number of mRNA regions crosslink to the silencing complex in vivo yet lack known site types matching the cognate miRNA.
source: The existence of additional, still-to-be-characterized types of non-canonical sites is suggested by the large number of mRNA regions that crosslink to the silencing complex in vivo yet lack known site types matching the cognate miRNA (Chi et al., 2012; Loeb et al., 2012; Helwak et al., 2013; Khorshid et al., 2013; Grosswendt et al., 2014).
evidence: This observation from CLIP studies is cited from multiple sources.

claim: The type of miRNA binding site strongly influences the efficacy of repression.
source: As previously mentioned, the type of site (e.g., whether the site is an 8mer or a 7mer-A1) strongly influences the efficacy of repression.
evidence: This is established knowledge referenced earlier in the text.

claim: Each additional miRNA binding site typically acts independently to impart additional repression.
source: The number of sites also influences efficacy, with each additional site typically acting independently to impart additional repression (Grimson et al., 2007; Nielsen et al., 2007)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: MicroRNA binding sites between 8-40 nt of each other tend to act cooperatively.
source: although sites between 8–40 nt of each other tend to act cooperatively, and those < 8 nt of each other act competitively (Grimson et al., 2007)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: MicroRNA binding sites less than 8 nt of each other act competitively.
source: sites between 8–40 nt of each other tend to act cooperatively, and those < 8 nt of each other act competitively (Grimson et al., 2007)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Sites positioned outside of the path of the ribosome (the first 15 nt of the 3′ UTR) are more effective.
source: These features include the positioning of the site outside of the path of the ribosome (which includes the first 15 nt of the 3′ UTR [Grimson et al., 2007])
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Sites within 3′-UTR segments with high local AU content are more accessible to the silencing complex.
source: the positioning of the site within 3′-UTR segments that are more accessible to the silencing complex, as measured by either high local AU content (Grimson et al., 2007; Nielsen et al., 2007)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Sites in 3′ UTRs with high overall AU content are more effective.
source: high AU content of the entire 3′ UTR (Robins and Press, 2005; Hausser et al., 2009)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Sites at shorter distance from a 3′-UTR terminus are more effective.
source: shorter distance from a 3′-UTR terminus (Gaidatzis et al., 2007; Grimson et al., 2007; Majoros and Ohler, 2007)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Sites in shorter 3′ UTRs are more effective.
source: shorter 3′-UTR length (Hausser et al., 2009; Betel et al., 2010; Wen et al., 2011; Reczko et al., 2012)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Sites with less stable predicted competing secondary structure are more effective.
source: less stable predicted competing secondary structure (Robins et al., 2005; Ameres et al., 2007; Kertesz et al., 2007; Long et al., 2007; Tafer et al., 2008)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Conserved sites are more effective, in part because they tend to reside in more favorable contexts.
source: Conserved sites are also more effective, in part because they tend to reside in more favorable contexts (Grimson et al., 2007; Nielsen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Sites are more effective if the miRNA has lower target-site abundance (TA) within the transcriptome.
source: Features of the miRNA can also influence site efficacy, with sites being more effective if the miRNA has lower target-site abundance (TA) within the transcriptome (Arvey et al., 2010; Garcia et al., 2011)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Sites are more effective if the miRNA has stronger predicted seed-pairing stability (SPS).
source: stronger predicted seed-pairing stability (SPS) (Garcia et al., 2011)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The context+ model considers features of the original context scores plus two miRNA features (TA and SPS).
source: Our recent model, called the context-plus (context+) model, considers the features of our original context scores (i.e., site type, 3′-supplementary pairing, local AU content, and distance from the closest 3′-UTR end [Grimson et al., 2007]), plus two miRNA features (TA and SPS [Garcia et al., 2011]).
evidence: This describes the previous model developed by the authors.

claim: The context+ model was trained using multiple regression on 74 high-throughput datasets.
source: Although the context+ model was trained using multiple regression on 74 high-throughput datasets
evidence: This describes the training of the previous model.

claim: The features used to distinguish effective sites in the context+ model were identified using only 11 datasets.
source: the features used to distinguish effective sites (the three features of the original context scores) were identified using only 11 datasets
evidence: This describes a limitation of the previous model.

claim: mRNAs with nucleation-bulge sites to miR-430 show no evidence of repression in zebrafish embryos.
source: Even in this system, one of the most sensitive systems for detecting the effects of targeting (where a robust repression is observed for mRNAs with only a single 6mer or offset-6mer sites to miR-430), we observed no evidence for repression of mRNAs with nucleation-bulge sites to miR-430 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding shown in Figure 1A and related supplementary figures.

claim: mRNAs with nucleation-bulge sites to miR-124 are no more repressed than mRNAs without sites.
source: However, even in this more limited context, the mRNAs with nucleation-bulge sites were no more repressed than mRNAs without sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: mRNAs with CLIP-supported non-canonical miR-155 sites show a distribution of fold changes that converges with the no-site distribution at the top of the curve.
source: However, for the mRNAs harboring non-canonical miR-155 sites, the distribution of fold changes converged with the no-site distribution at the top of the curve (Figure 1B)
evidence: This observation is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: mRNAs with non-canonical miR-155 sites showed no evidence of derepression in Th1, Th2, and B cells lacking miR-155.
source: In contrast to mRNAs with canonical sites, the mRNAs with non-canonical sites showed no evidence of derepression in the knockout cells of each of these cell types, which reinforced the conclusion that non-canonical binding of miR-155 does not lead to repression of these mRNAs (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: mRNAs with CLASH-identified non-canonical miR-92 interactions show a distribution of fold changes that converges with the no-site distribution.
source: However, a closer look at the mRNA fold-change distributions again revealed a pattern not typically observed for mRNAs with a functional site type, with convergence with the no-site distribution in the region expected to be most divergent.
evidence: This observation is described in the context of Figure 1D.

claim: The slight up-regulation of mRNAs with CLASH-identified non-canonical miR-92 interactions was not reproducible in a second dataset.
source: As reported recently (Wang, 2014), the slight up-regulation observed for mRNAs with CLASH-identified non-canonical interactions in the original dataset was not reproducible in the second dataset (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and cited from another study.

claim: mRNAs with non-canonical interactions to other miRNAs showed no sign of derepression when the cognate miRNAs were knocked down.
source: Moreover, mRNAs with non-canonical interactions to other miRNAs showed no sign of derepression when the cognate miRNAs were knocked down (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: mRNAs with chimera-identified canonical sites tend to be derepressed upon miRNA knockdown, whereas those with only non-canonical sites do not.
source: Indeed, when we re-examined the response of these mRNAs to miRNA knockdown, those with chimera-identified canonical sites tended to be derepressed, whereas those with only chimera-identified non-canonical sites did not (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F and supplementary figures.

claim: The conservation signal of chimera-identified non-canonical sites is not smaller for sites of less conserved miRNAs.
source: we found that this conservation signal was not smaller for the sites of less conserved miRNAs and therefore was not indicative of functional miRNA binding (Figure 1—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This analysis is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Top non-canonical MIRZA targets without 6mer or offset-6mer seed matches show no sign of efficacy.
source: Indeed, when focusing on only targets without 6mer or offset-6mer seed matches, the top 100 non-canonical MIRZA targets showed no sign of efficacy (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G.

claim: mRNAs with IMPACT-seq-supported non-canonical sites responded no differently than mRNAs lacking a site upon miRNA transfection.
source: Although the mRNAs with an IMPACT-seq–supported canonical site were down-regulated upon the transfection of the cognate miRNA, those with an IMPACT-seq–supported non-canonical site responded no differently than mRNAs lacking a site (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H.

claim: CLIP-identified non-canonical sites impart no detectable repression when monitoring mRNA changes.
source: Collectively, the novel non-canonical sites recently identified in high-throughput CLIP and other biochemical studies imparted no detectable repression when monitoring mRNA changes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analyses in Figure 1.

claim: CLIP-identified non-canonical sites impart no detectable repression when monitoring ribosome profiling and proteomic data.
source: To address this possibility, we examined ribosome-profiling and proteomic datasets, which capture repression also occurring at the level of translation, and again we found that the CLIP-identified non-canonical sites imparted no detectable repression (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1I and supplementary figures.

claim: In mammals, canonical sites to the same miRNA typically act independently.
source: However, in mammals, canonical sites to the same miRNA typically act independently (Grimson et al., 2007; Nielsen et al., 2007)
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: dCLIP clusters without cognate seed matches are enriched for imperfect pairing to the miRNA.
source: The inefficacy of recently reported non-canonical sites was surprising when considering evidence that the dCLIP clusters without cognate seed matches are nonetheless enriched for imperfect pairing to the miRNA, which would not be expected if those clusters were merely non-specific background (Chi et al., 2012; Loeb et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous CLIP studies.

claim: The top motif identified within miR-124 dCLIP clusters lacking a canonical site has striking complementarity to the miR-124 seed region.
source: the top motif, as identified by MEME (Bailey and Elkan, 1994), had striking complementarity to the miR-124 seed region (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A using motif analysis.

claim: The human miR-124 non-canonical motif matches the nucleation-bulge motif originally found for miR-124 in the mouse brain.
source: This human miR-124 non-canonical motif matched the 'nucleation-bulge' motif originally found for miR-124 in the mouse brain (Chi et al., 2012).
evidence: This comparison is made to previous findings.

claim: The top motif identified within miR-155 dCLIP clusters lacking a canonical site has only a single mismatch to the miR-155 seed.
source: Although the top motif identified within the subset of miR-155 dCLIP clusters that lacked a canonical site to miR-155 was not identified with confidence, it had only a single mismatch to the miR-155 seed
evidence: This is described in the context of Figure 2A.

claim: CLASH-identified interactions without canonical sites are enriched for motifs that pair to the miRNA, often outside the seed region.
source: Previous analysis of CLASH-identified interactions shows that the top MEME-identified motifs usually pair to the miRNA, although for many miRNAs this pairing falls outside of the seed region (Helwak et al., 2013). Repeating this analysis, but focusing on only interactions without canonical sites, confirmed this result (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and cited from previous work.

claim: Chimera-identified interactions are more specific to the seed region than CLASH-identified interactions.
source: As previously shown (Grosswendt et al., 2014), these interactions were more specific to the seed region than were the CLASH-identified interactions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and cited from previous work.

claim: A higher fraction of chimera data captured canonical interactions compared to CLASH data.
source: Comparison of all the chimera data with all the CLASH data showed that a higher fraction of the chimeras captured canonical interactions and that a higher fraction captured interactions within 3′ UTRs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This comparison is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Chimera-identified non-canonical interactions in human and nematode datasets are enriched for motifs that pair to the miRNA seed region.
source: In the human and nematode datasets (and less so in the mouse dataset), these interactions were enriched for motifs that corresponded to non-canonical sites that paired to the miRNA seed region (Figure 2B–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B-C and supplementary figures.

claim: The most enriched nucleotides in non-canonical binding motifs typically preserve Watson-Crick pairing in a core 4-5 nts within the seed region.
source: Inspection of these motifs revealed that the most enriched nucleotides typically preserved Watson–Crick pairing in a core 4–5 nts within the seed region, with tolerance to mismatches or G:U wobbles observed at varied positions
evidence: This is inferred from inspection of motifs shown in figures.

claim: Motifs for only a few miRNAs had a bulged nucleotide, and bulges were in the mRNA strand, not the miRNA strand.
source: Motifs for only a few miRNAs had a bulged nucleotide, and if a bulge was observed it was in the mRNA strand and not in the miRNA strand, as expected if the Argonaute protein imposed geometric constraints in the seed of the miRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from motif analysis.

claim: The miR-124 nucleation-bulge site was enriched in mouse chimera interactions.
source: The miR-124 nucleation-bulge site was enriched in mouse chimera interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The miR-124 nucleation-bulge style of bulged pairing was not detected for any other miRNA.
source: However, despite identification of this miR-124 interaction in datasets from two methods and two species, this style of bulged pairing was not detected for any other miRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the motif analysis across multiple miRNAs.

claim: For miRNAs other than miR-124 with bulges in recognition motifs, the bulge was between nucleotides pairing to miRNA positions 4 and 5.
source: Interestingly, for all other cases in which a bulge in the recognition motif was observed (human miR-33 and miR-374, and C. elegans miR-50 and miR-58), the bulge was between the nucleotides that paired to miRNA nucleotides 4 and 5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: A bulge between target nucleotides pairing to miRNA positions 4 and 5 is observed in validated targets of Arabidopsis miR398.
source: A bulge is observed between the analogous nucleotides of validated targets of Arabidopsis miR398 (Jones-Rhoades and Bartel, 2004)
evidence: This is cited from previous work on plant miRNAs.

claim: A bulge between target nucleotides pairing to miRNA positions 4 and 5 is observed in the first let-7 site in C. elegans lin-41 3′ UTR.
source: A bulge between these nucleotides is also observed in the first let-7 site in the C. elegans lin-41 3′ UTR, one of the archetypal 3′-compensatory sites (Reinhart et al., 2000; Bartel, 2009).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The most tolerated bulge in miRNA seed pairing is between target nucleotides that pair to miRNA nucleotides 4 and 5.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that the most tolerated bulge in miRNA seed pairing is between the target nucleotides that pair to miRNA nucleotides 4 and 5.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple observations across species.

claim: Many CLIP clusters and CLASH/chimera interactions lacking a seed match capture authentic miRNA-binding sites.
source: In sum, our analyses of the CLIP datasets confirmed that many of the CLIP clusters and CLASH/chimera interactions lacking a seed match nonetheless capture authentic miRNA-binding sites—otherwise the top enriched motifs would not pair so often to the cognate miRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the motif enrichment analysis.

claim: CLIP-identified non-canonical sites bind miRNA in vivo and contribute to cellular target-site abundance but do not mediate repression.
source: Despite this ability to bind the miRNA in vivo and to function in the sense that they contribute to cellular TA (Denzler et al., 2014), we classify the CLIP-identified non-canonical sites as non-functional with respect to repression because they showed no sign of mediating repression and no signal for miRNA-dependent conservation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined evidence of binding (Figure 2) and lack of repression (Figure 1).

claim: The only known non-canonical site types that mediate repression are 3′-supplementary, centered, and cleavage sites, which comprise less than 1% of effective sites.
source: Thus, the only known non-canonical site types that mediate repression are the 3′-supplementary, centered, and cleavage site types, which together comprise <1% of the effective sites that currently can be predicted (Friedman et al., 2009; Shin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: mRNA fold changes of some arrays were highly correlated despite different transfected sRNAs, indicating sRNA-independent effects.
source: Despite the differences among the 74 transfected sRNAs, mRNA fold changes of some arrays were highly correlated with those of others, which indicated that sRNA-independent effects dominated (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Datasets from the same group or transfection protocol clustered strongly together, indicating likely batch effects.
source: When all 74 datasets were compared against each other, those from either the same group of experiments (Anderson et al., 2008) or the same transfection protocol (Jackson et al., 2006a, 2006b; Grimson et al., 2007) tended to cluster strongly together based on their common transcriptome-wide responses to different transfected sRNAs (Figure 3B), indicating the likely presence of batch effects (Leek et al., 2010)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and cited regarding batch effects.

claim: 3′-UTR AU content often correlated with mRNA fold changes for mRNAs without a canonical site to the transfected sRNA.
source: Indeed, when considering mRNAs without a canonical site to the transfected sRNA, we found that 3′-UTR AU content often correlated with mRNA fold changes.
evidence: This is described in the context of Figure 3C.

claim: The extent and direction of correlation between 3′-UTR AU content and mRNA fold changes was similar for datasets from the same publication but differed between publications.
source: Moreover, the extent and direction of the correlation was similar for different datasets from the same publication but differed when comparing to datasets from other publications (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 3′-UTR length exhibited patterns of correlation with mRNA fold changes similar to those observed for 3′-UTR AU content.
source: A second parameter that helped explain the correlated sRNA-independent effects for related datasets was 3′-UTR length (Saito and Satrom, 2012), which exhibited patterns of correlation similar to those observed for 3′-UTR AU content (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and cited from previous work.

claim: Derepression of mRNAs with sites for endogenous miRNAs occurs, presumably through competition for limiting silencing pathway components.
source: Another phenomenon known to systematically perturb the levels of mRNAs without sites to the transfected sRNA is the derepression of mRNAs with sites for endogenous miRNAs, presumably through competition between the transfected sRNA and the endogenous miRNAs for limiting components of the silencing pathway (Khan et al., 2009; Saito and Satrom, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Statistically significant derepression was observed for mRNAs with sites to eight of the 10 most frequently sequenced miRNA families in HeLa cells.
source: Statistically significant derepression was indeed observed for mRNAs with sites to eight of the 10 miRNA families most frequently sequenced in HeLa cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Applying PLSR normalization largely eliminated correlations between datasets.
source: Applying our technique to all the mRNAs in each of the 74 datasets largely eliminated the correlations observed between datasets (Figure 3D–E)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: PLSR normalization eliminated correlations between mRNA fold changes and either AU content or 3′-UTR length.
source: as well as the correlations observed between mRNA fold changes and either AU content or 3′-UTR length (Figure 3F)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: PLSR normalization eliminated the signal for derepression of endogenous miRNA targets.
source: Moreover, our technique eliminated the signal for derepression of endogenous miRNA targets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Reducing biases through normalization substantially enhanced the net signal for sRNA-mediated repression.
source: Reducing these biases substantially reduced the variance in the response for mRNAs without sites to the sRNA, which substantially enhanced the net signal for sRNA-mediated repression of site-containing mRNAs observed in individual arrays (Figure 3G) and all arrays in aggregate (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: The presence of multiple abundant 3′-UTR isoforms for a gene confounds interpretation of 3′-UTR-related features.
source: The presence of more than one abundant 3′-UTR isoform for a gene would confound interpretation of 3′-UTR-related features, such as 3′-UTR length, or distance from the closest 3′-UTR end (Nam et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: Shorter 3′-UTR isoforms might not include some target sites, causing these sites to appear ineffective when they are not present.
source: Moreover, the shorter 3′-UTR isoforms might not include some target sites, which would cause these sites to appear ineffective when in fact they are not present (Sandberg et al., 2008; Mayr and Bartel, 2009; Lianoglou et al., 2013; Nam et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The model was developed using mRNAs from genes where ≥90% of 3P-seq tags corresponded to a single 3′-UTR isoform.
source: To avoid these complications, we examined 3′-UTR isoform quantifications previously generated for HeLa cells (Nam et al., 2014) using poly(A)-position profiling by sequencing (3P-seq) (Jan et al., 2011), and developed our model using the dominant mRNA from the subset of genes for which ≥90% of the 3P-seq tags corresponded to a single 3′-UTR isoform.
evidence: This describes the methodology for selecting mRNAs for model development.

claim: The model was developed using mRNAs with a single seed match to the transfected sRNA in the 3′ UTR.
source: To isolate the effects of single sites, we also used the subset of these mRNAs for which the 3′ UTR possessed a single seed match to the transfected sRNA (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the methodology for selecting mRNAs for model development.

claim: 26 features were considered as potentially informative of miRNA targeting efficacy.
source: To improve our model of mammalian target-site efficacy, we considered 26 features as potentially informative of efficacy.
evidence: This is stated in the text and detailed in Table 1.

claim: 14 features were robustly selected through stepwise regression in nearly all bootstrap samples for at least two site types.
source: Reasoning that features most predictive would be robustly selected, we focused on 14 features selected in nearly all 1000 bootstrap samples for at least two site types (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 1.

claim: The 14 selected features include site type, 3′-supplementary pairing, local AU content, distance from 3′-UTR ends, TA, SPS, 3′-UTR length, ORF length, predicted structural accessibility, number of offset-6mer sites in 3′ UTR, number of 8mer sites in ORF, nucleotide identity of position 8 of the target, nucleotide identity of positions 1 and 8 of the sRNA, and site conservation.
source: These included all three features considered in our original context-only model (minimum distance from 3′-UTR ends, local AU composition and 3′-supplementary pairing), the two added in our context+ model (SPS and TA), as well as nine additional features (3′-UTR length, ORF length, predicted SA, the number of offset-6mer sites in the 3′ UTR and 8mer sites in the ORF, the nucleotide identity of position 8 of the target, the nucleotide identity of positions 1 and 8 of the sRNA, and site conservation).
evidence: This lists the features selected, as shown in Table 1.

claim: mRNAs with longer ORFs tend to be more resistant to miRNA-mediated repression.
source: For example, mRNAs with either longer ORFs or longer 3′ UTRs tended to be more resistant to repression (indicated by a positive coefficient)
evidence: This is inferred from the positive regression coefficient shown in Figure 4C.

claim: mRNAs with longer 3′ UTRs tend to be more resistant to miRNA-mediated repression.
source: For example, mRNAs with either longer ORFs or longer 3′ UTRs tended to be more resistant to repression (indicated by a positive coefficient)
evidence: This is inferred from the positive regression coefficient shown in Figure 4C.

claim: mRNAs with structurally accessible target sites tend to be more prone to miRNA-mediated repression.
source: whereas mRNAs with either structurally accessible target sites or ORF 8mer sites tended to be more prone to repression (indicated by a negative coefficient)
evidence: This is inferred from the negative regression coefficient shown in Figure 4C.

claim: mRNAs with ORF 8mer sites tend to be more prone to miRNA-mediated repression.
source: whereas mRNAs with either structurally accessible target sites or ORF 8mer sites tended to be more prone to repression (indicated by a negative coefficient)
evidence: This is inferred from the negative regression coefficient shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 3′-UTR length, ORF length, and structural accessibility contribute similarly to features previously incorporated in the context+ model.
source: Based on the relative magnitudes of the regression coefficients, some newly incorporated features, such as 3′-UTR length, ORF length, and SA, contributed similarly to features previously incorporated in the context+ model, such as SPS, TA, and local AU (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing coefficient magnitudes in Figure 4C.

claim: The presence of a 5′ G in the sRNA is associated with reduced site efficacy.
source: New features with an intermediate level of influence included the number of ORF 8mer sites and site conservation as well as the presence of a 5′ G in the sRNA (Figure 4C), the latter perhaps a consequence of differential sRNA loading efficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the regression coefficients in Figure 4C and speculated about loading efficiency.

claim: A position-8 C in the sRNA further decreases efficacy of 6mer or 7mer-A1 sites relative to a position-8 U.
source: Relative to a position-8 U in the sRNA, a position-8 C further decreased efficacy of sites with a mismatch at this position (6mer or 7mer-A1 sites), whereas a position-8 A had the opposite effect (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A position-8 A in the sRNA increases efficacy of 6mer or 7mer-A1 sites relative to a position-8 U.
source: Relative to a position-8 U in the sRNA, a position-8 C further decreased efficacy of sites with a mismatch at this position (6mer or 7mer-A1 sites), whereas a position-8 A had the opposite effect (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A position-8 C in the target site confers decreased efficacy of 6mer and 7mer-A1 sites relative to a position-8 U.
source: Similarly, a position-8 C in the site also conferred decreased efficacy of 6mer and 7mer-A1 sites relative to a position-8 U in the site (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The context++ model was compared to 17 in silico tools for predicting miRNA targets.
source: We compared the predictive performance of our context++ model to that of the most recent versions of 17 in silico tools for predicting miRNA targets
evidence: The comparison is described and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The context++ model performed substantially better than the most predictive published model (TargetScan6.All) when predicting repression of mRNAs with canonical 7-8 nt 3′-UTR sites.
source: The context++ model performed substantially better than the most predictive published model, which was TargetScan6.All.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: DIANA-microT-CDS, miRTarget2, miRanda-miRSVR, MIRZA-G, and TargetRank were the most predictive algorithms from other groups.
source: Of algorithms derived from other groups, DIANA-microT-CDS, miRTarget2, miRanda-miRSVR, MIRZA-G (and its derivatives), and TargetRank were the most predictive, with performance within range of TargetScan5.All (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: All algorithms designed to identify many non-canonical sites performed poorly in predicting the response of mRNAs lacking canonical 7-8 nt 3′-UTR sites.
source: However, all of these algorithms performed poorly in predicting the response of mRNAs lacking such sites (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The context++ model achieved modest prediction accuracy for mRNAs lacking canonical 7-8 nt 3′-UTR sites by capturing effects of canonical 6mers.
source: The two algorithms achieving any semblance of prediction accuracy did so by predicting some of the canonical interactions with known marginal efficacy. These were DIANA-microT-CDS, which captured modest effects of canonical sites in ORFs (Reczko et al., 2012; Marin et al., 2013), and the context++ model, which captured the modest effects of canonical 6mers in 3′ UTRs (as modified by the 14 features, which included offset 6mers and 8mer ORF sites) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Algorithms designed to identify many non-canonical sites had r² < 0.004 when predicting mRNAs without canonical 7-8 nt sites.
source: The algorithms designed to identify many non-canonical sites performed much more poorly in this test (r2 < 0.004)
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 5C results.

claim: The top 112 predictions of the context++ model (average of 16 per miRNA) were significantly more repressed than top predictions from earlier TargetScan versions.
source: When choosing an average of 16 predicted targets for each of the seven test-set miRNAs, we found that these top 112 predictions of the context++ model were significantly more repressed than the top predictions from earlier versions of TargetScan (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The top 112 predictions of the context++ model were significantly more repressed than top predictions of other algorithms.
source: and the top predictions of the other algorithms (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The distribution of fold changes for top context++ predictions intersected 0.0 at a cumulative fraction of 0.92, indicating 8% of top predictions increased rather than decreased.
source: Despite the success of the context++ model, not all of the fold changes for its top predicted targets were negative; for the test set, the distribution of these fold changes intersected 0.0 at a cumulative fraction of 0.92, indicating that mRNAs for 8% of the top predictions increased rather than decreased with transfection of the cognate miRNA (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The upper limit estimate for false-positive predictions of the context++ model is 16% at the cutoff of 16 predictions per miRNA.
source: Because only half of the false-positive predictions would be expected to have positive fold changes in the presence of the miRNA, our best estimate of the upper limit on the false-positive predictions was 2 × 8%, or 16%, at this cutoff
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Figure 5D.

claim: Previous algorithms had upper limit estimates for false positives ranging from 24-100% at the same cutoff.
source: At the same cutoff, the distribution of fold changes for each of the previous algorithms intersected 0.0 at a cumulative fractions ranging from 0.50–0.88 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), which implied lower prediction specificity than that observed for the context++ model, with correspondingly higher estimates for the upper limits of false positives among their top predictions, ranging from 24–100%.
evidence: This is shown in supplementary figures and calculated from the data.

claim: Regardless of the cutoff, the top context++ predictions were the most repressed across a broad spectrum of cutoffs.
source: To evaluate the performance of top-ranked predictions more systematically, we examined median repression of the predicted targets over a broad spectrum of cutoffs, ranging from an average of 4–4096 predictions per miRNA (Figure 5E). Regardless of the cutoff, the top context++ predictions were the most repressed.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The top predictions of most other algorithms were repressed significantly more than expected by chance.
source: The top predictions of most other algorithms were repressed significantly more than expected by chance
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The median repression of top predictions from MBSTAR, RNA22, PACCMIT-CDS, and AnTarCLIP did not exceed the median repression of all mRNAs with a canonical 7-8 nt 3′-UTR site.
source: although the median repression of some (MBSTAR, RNA22, PACCMIT-CDS, and AnTarCLIP) did not exceed the median repression of all mRNAs with a canonical 7–8 nt 3′-UTR site (Figure 5E)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: After eliminating canonical 7-8 nt 3′-UTR sites, the remaining top predictions were modestly repressed at best.
source: After eliminating interactions that could involve canonical 7–8 nt 3′-UTR sites, the remaining top predictions were modestly repressed at best (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F and supplementary figures.

claim: The most repressed predicted targets without canonical 7-8 nt 3′-UTR sites were those of the context++ model, which scored predictions with canonical 6mer 3′-UTR sites.
source: The most repressed predicted targets without canonical 7–8 nt 3′-UTR sites were those of the context++ model, which scored predictions with canonical 6mer 3′-UTR sites.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 5F results.

claim: For algorithms designed to identify many non-canonical sites, the top predictions without 7-8 nt 3′-UTR sites were essentially unresponsive to the transfected miRNA.
source: For algorithms designed to identify many non-canonical sites, the top predictions without 7–8 nt 3′-UTR sites were essentially unresponsive to the transfected miRNA
evidence: This is stated in the text describing Figure 5F results.

claim: TargetScan7 predictions performed at least as well as canonical CLIP-supported targets in all comparisons.
source: Regardless of the set of canonical CLIP-supported targets examined, we did not find a setting in which they responded significantly better than did the cohort of TargetScan7 predictions, and in some cases, the TargetScan7 predictions performed significantly better (Figure 6A–J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A-J.

claim: TargetScan7 predictions performed at least as well as mRNAs identified by pulldown-seq or IMPACT-seq with canonical sites.
source: Similar results were observed when comparing the repression of our predictions to that of mRNAs identified biochemically without crosslinking, using either pulldown-seq or IMPACT-seq (Tan et al., 2014), again focusing on only mRNAs with canonical sites (Figure 6K,L).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6K-L.

claim: For identifying consequential miRNA-target interactions, the TargetScan7 model is more convenient than experimental determination of binding sites and at least as effective.
source: Thus, for identifying consequential miRNA–target interactions, the TargetScan7 model is not only more convenient than experimental determination of binding sites, it is also at least as effective.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparisons in Figure 6.

claim: The context++ model explained 14% of the variability observed among mRNAs with canonical 7-8 nt 3′-UTR sites in the test set.
source: Yet despite applying this same normalization procedure to our test set, the observed r2 value of 0.14 implied that our model explained only 14% of the variability observed among mRNAs with canonical 7–8 nt 3′-UTR sites (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated based on the r² value shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The r² value increased to 0.15 when considering the usage of alternative 3′-UTR isoforms.
source: The r2 value increased to 0.15 when considering the usage of alternative 3′-UTR isoforms
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: A model trained on only site type and the other 13 molecular features (excluding PCT) performed nearly as well as the full context++ model.
source: Moreover, when tested as in Figure 5B, a model trained on only site type and the other 13 molecular features performed nearly as well as the full context++ model (r2 of 0.126, compared to 0.139 for the full model).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the text.

claim: The context++ model captured 70% of the information potentially imparted by molecular features when predicting test-set mRNAs with major canonical site types.
source: This drop in r2 of only 0.013 was substantially less than the 0.044 r2 observed for the site-conservation feature on its own (Figure 5B, TargetScan.PCT), which suggested that when predicting the response of the test-set mRNAs with the major canonical site types, the context++ model captured 70% (calculated as [0.044–0.013]/0.044) of the information potentially imparted by molecular features.
evidence: This is calculated from the r² values.

claim: The context++ model is generally applicable to all canonical sites, including nonconserved sites and sites for nonconserved miRNAs.
source: Its general applicability to all canonical sites is useful for evaluating not only nonconserved sites to conserved miRNAs but also all sites for nonconserved miRNAs (e.g., Figure 6K,L), including viral miRNAs, as well as the off-targets of synthetic siRNAs and shRNAs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the model's applicability.

claim: Recent computational and experimental approaches fail to identify non-canonical targets that are repressed more than control transcripts.
source: Our analyses show that recent computational and experimental approaches, including the different types of CLIP, all fail to identify non-canonical targets that are repressed more than control transcripts (Figures 1, 5C,F)
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from multiple figures.

claim: CLIP approaches can identify non-canonical sites that bind the miRNA with some degree of specificity.
source: Although CLIP approaches can identify non-canonical sites that bind the miRNA with some degree of specificity (Figure 2)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2.

claim: CLIP-identified non-canonical binding sites do not function to mediate detectable repression.
source: these non-canonical binding sites do not function to mediate detectable repression
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analyses in Figure 1.

claim: The inability of CLIP approaches to identify non-canonical targets that are repressed more than controls argues strongly against the existence of many functional non-canonical targets.
source: Therefore, our analyses of the CLIP results, which detected no residual repression after accounting for canonical interactions, provide the most compelling evidence to date on this issue. Unless there is a substantial technical bias in the CLIP approach (such as a large unanticipated disparity in the propensity of non-canonical interactions to crosslink), the inability of current CLIP approaches to identify non-canonical targets that are repressed more than control transcripts argues strongly against the existence of many functional non-canonical targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CLIP analyses.

claim: CLIP-identified non-canonical sites in 3′ UTRs bind the miRNA too transiently to mediate repression.
source: Therefore, a more plausible explanation is that the CLIP-identified non-canonical sites bind the miRNA too transiently to mediate repression.
evidence: This is proposed as an explanation for the inefficacy of non-canonical sites.

claim: The high abundance of non-canonical binding sites helps offset their low occupancy, yielding more non-canonical than canonical sites detected by CLIP.
source: The motifs identified in the non-canonical interactions have information contents as low as 5.6 bits, and thus are much more common in 3′ UTRs than canonical 6mer or 7mer sites (12 bits and 14 bits, respectively). This high abundance of the non-canonical binding sites would help offset the low occupancy of individual non-canonical sites, such that at any moment more than half of the bound miRNA might reside at non-canonical sites, yielding more non-canonical than canonical sites when using experimental approaches with such high specificity that they can identify a site with only a single read
evidence: This is an explanation proposed based on information theory and CLIP data.

claim: Variable crosslinking efficiency might explain why many ineffective non-canonical sites are identified by CLIP.
source: When considered together with the high abundance of non-canonical sites, variable crosslinking efficiency might explain why so many ineffective non-canonical sites are identified. Overlaying a wide distribution of crosslinking efficiencies onto the many thousands of ineffective, non-canonical sites could yield a substantial number of sites at the high-efficiency tail of the distribution for which the tag support matches that of effective canonical sites.
evidence: This is proposed as an explanation for CLIP results.

claim: Variable crosslinking efficiency explains why many top predictions of the context++ model are missed by CLIP methods.
source: Variable crosslinking efficiency also explains why many top predictions of the context++ model are missed by the CLIP methods, as indicated by the modest overlap in the CLIP identified targets and the top predictions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is proposed as an explanation based on the overlap shown in Figure 6.

claim: The requirement of extensive additional pairing to compensate for a seed mismatch arises from several sources including unfavorable conformational changes and relative disorder of 3′ nucleotides.
source: The requirement of so much additional pairing to make up for a single mismatch to the seed is proposed to arise from several sources. The advantage of propagating continuous pairing past miRNA nucleotide 8 (as occurs for centered sites) might be largely offset by the cost of an unfavorable conformational change (Bartel, 2009; Schirle et al., 2014). Likewise, the advantage of resuming pairing at the miRNA 3′ region (as occurs for 3′-compensatory sites) might be partially offset by either the relative disorder of these nucleotides (Bartel, 2009) or their unfavorable arrangement prior to seed pairing (Schirle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous structural and mechanistic work.

claim: The seed backbone is pre-organized to favor A-form pairing, with bases of nucleotides 2-5 accessible to nucleate pairing.
source: In contrast, the seed backbone is pre-organized to favor A-form pairing, with bases of nucleotides 2–5 accessible to nucleate pairing (Nakanishi et al., 2012; Schirle and MacRae, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from structural studies.

claim: Perfect pairing propagated through miRNA nucleotide 7 creates the opportunity for favorable contacts to the minor groove of the seed:target duplex.
source: Moreover, perfect pairing propagated through miRNA nucleotide 7 creates the opportunity for favorable contacts to the minor groove of the seed:target duplex (Schirle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from structural work.

claim: TargetScan version 7.0 integrated the context++ model with current 3′-UTR-isoform data.
source: Our overhaul of the TargetScan website integrated the output of the context++ model with the most current 3′-UTR-isoform data
evidence: This describes the implementation of TargetScan7.

claim: The number of human 3′-UTR sites conserved above background increased from approximately 46,400 to approximately 62,300 with updated PCT scores.
source: Using these updates increased sensitivity, with our estimate for the number of human 3′-UTR sites conserved above background increasing from ∼46,400 (Friedman et al., 2009) to ∼62,300.
evidence: This is stated as a result of updating PCT scores.

claim: Predicted structural accessibility was scored as proportional to the log10 value of the unpaired probability for a 14-nt region centered on the match to miRNA nucleotides 7 and 8.
source: Based on these results, which resembled those reported previously (Tafer et al., 2008), we scored predicted structural accessibility (SA) as proportional to the log10 value of the unpaired probability for a 14-nt region centered on the match to miRNA nucleotides 7 and 8.
evidence: This describes the methodology for scoring SA based on analysis shown in Figure 4A.
